m7-t1.introduction: Build a permission-based relationship after the first click. See the sender, message and measurement as one system rather than a list of addresses.

sections.title: Email connects the second half of the funnel
sections.explanation: Acquisition starts the relationship; useful follow-up helps people act, succeed and return.

items.label: Enquiry
items.detail: Answer an unresolved question with relevant information.

items.label: First purchase
items.detail: Confirm and help the customer get value.

items.label: Repeat relationship
items.detail: Offer relevant updates at the agreed cadence.

items.label: Re-engagement / exit
items.detail: Re-earn attention or respect the decision to leave.

sections.takeaway: A contact address is not blanket permission for any future promotion.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The strategic role: retention and repeat

sections.title: Deliverability has four foundations
sections.explanation: A sending tool is only one part of a responsible email programme.

items.label: Tool
items.detail: Use an appropriate provider with the needed controls.

items.label: Sender identity
items.detail: Configure the required domain authentication using current provider guidance.

items.label: Permission
items.detail: Record the purpose, source and scope of signup.

items.label: Hygiene
items.detail: Handle hard bounces, complaints and suppression promptly.

sections.takeaway: Provider requirements vary by sender and change over time. An authentication check does not guarantee inbox placement.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. The mechanics: tool, sender, list

sections.title: Five email jobs to master first
sections.explanation: Each email needs a reason to exist from the recipient’s point of view.

items.label: Welcome
items.detail: Deliver the promised resource and set expectations.

items.label: Newsletter
items.detail: Offer repeatable useful value at the agreed cadence.

items.label: Offer
items.detail: Explain one genuine promotion with clear conditions.

items.label: Win-back
items.detail: Invite a dormant subscriber back, then stop if the agreed series ends.

items.label: Receipt / onboarding
items.detail: Confirm the transaction and help the customer succeed.

sections.takeaway: Transactional messages and promotional messages have different purposes; do not hide marketing inside a necessary service message.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The five emails every business needs

sections.title: An email is a promise-to-action path
sections.explanation: The subject and preview earn attention, while the body delivers the promised value.

items.label: Subject + preview
items.detail: State a specific, honest reason to open.

items.label: One useful idea
items.detail: Make the meaning easy to scan.

items.label: One primary CTA
items.detail: Name the appropriate next step.

items.label: Identity + exit
items.detail: Make the sender and withdrawal route easy to find.

sections.takeaway: Read the email on a phone and test every link before sending.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. The repeatable structure

sections.title: Read the denominator and the limitation
sections.explanation: Rates become useful only when you know what the provider actually counts.

items.label: Delivery
items.detail: Usually accepted delivery ÷ attempted sends; not proof of inbox placement.

items.label: Opens
items.detail: Often opens ÷ delivered; privacy features and image loading can distort it.

items.label: Clicks
items.detail: Check unique versus total clicks and the denominator; automated activity can affect counts.

items.label: Unsubscribes / complaints
items.detail: Watch for expectation or relevance problems and suppress appropriately.

sections.takeaway: Use your own history and current provider guidance. The visual layer does not treat a universal benchmark as a promise.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Does a 98% delivery rate prove 98% of messages reached the inbox?
checkpoint.answer: No. A provider’s delivery count generally means accepted rather than bounced. Inbox placement, spam filtering and engagement are different questions.

sections.section: 5. The four metrics and honest benchmarks

m7-t2.introduction: Draw lifecycle journeys before building them in a tool. Every journey needs a trigger, useful steps, an exit and suppression rules.

sections.title: A lifecycle map explains the next useful job
sections.explanation: The same message is not useful to a new subscriber, an active customer and someone who has withdrawn consent.

items.label: Subscriber
items.detail: Deliver the promise and explain the relationship.

items.label: Lead
items.detail: Answer objections and invite a suitable next step.

items.label: Customer
items.detail: Onboard and help the person succeed.

items.label: Active / dormant
items.detail: Support repeat value or a limited re-engagement route.

items.label: Exit
items.detail: Respect withdrawal and apply the appropriate suppression.

sections.takeaway: Business lifecycle stages and permission status are related but not interchangeable.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The lifecycle map

sections.title: Trigger → steps → exit, with guardrails
sections.explanation: A complete automation includes the conditions under which it must stop sending.

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: A permitted action starts the right journey.

items.label: Delay / branch
items.detail: Wait deliberately and choose a labelled path.

items.label: Goal / exit
items.detail: Stop selling once the person completes the intended action.

items.label: Suppression
items.detail: Prevent conflicting messages and honour opt-outs at every step.

sections.takeaway: Check exit and suppression conditions before each send, not just at enrolment.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Journey anatomy: trigger → steps → exit

sections.title: Build three clear journeys before a complex web
sections.explanation: Start with a small number of well-defined journeys that correspond to genuine customer needs.

items.label: Welcome series
items.detail: Deliver value, introduce the business and make a gentle next-step invitation.

items.label: Lead nurture
items.detail: Answer one real objection at a time and stop when the goal is reached.

items.label: Win-back
items.detail: Make a limited useful invitation, then exit or suppress as planned.

sections.takeaway: A longer sequence is not necessarily a more effective sequence.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The three core journeys (build these first)

sections.title: Relevant does not have to feel intrusive
sections.explanation: Use permitted behaviour to select a helpful message without narrating surveillance.

items.label: Creepy framing
items.detail: “We watched you revisit our pricing page six times.”

items.label: Helpful framing
items.detail: “Still comparing options? Here is the fee and batch guide.”

items.label: Data restraint
items.detail: Use only permitted, necessary signals and respect the person’s choice.

sections.takeaway: Personalisation should reduce effort for the recipient, not demonstrate how much the business knows.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. Behavioural triggers: personal without being creepy

sections.title: Count progress across the whole journey
sections.explanation: A journey-level goal rate is the final goal completions divided by eligible entrants, not the last email’s click rate.

items.label: Eligible entrants
items.detail: Synthetic leads joining one defined nurture journey.

items.label: Demo bookings
items.detail: 20% of eligible entrants book.

items.label: Enrolments
items.detail: 25% of bookings enrol; 5% of all entrants.

sections.takeaway: Track drop-off, exits and suppression alongside goal conversions. Do not force people through every step after they have already acted.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

checkpoint.question: A lead enrols after the first nurture message. Should the remaining sales sequence continue?
checkpoint.answer: No. The goal exit should stop that sales sequence. Apply the appropriate onboarding journey only where permitted, and prevent conflicting campaigns.

sections.section: 5. Measure journeys, not emails

m7-t3.introduction: A CRM is a shared memory of status, history and the next action. Make the pipeline reflect real decisions and keep follow-up accountable.

sections.title: The smallest useful CRM record
sections.explanation: Start with a record that stops enquiries being lost between people, not with a complex dashboard.

items.label: Status
items.detail: What stage is the enquiry actually at?

items.label: History
items.detail: What happened, when and through which permitted channel?

items.label: Owner
items.detail: Who is responsible for the next step?

items.label: Permission / access
items.detail: What contact is allowed, and who can see the record?

sections.takeaway: Collect only the fields needed for the purpose and control access to customer data.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. What a CRM is, honestly

sections.title: A stage needs an entry rule
sections.explanation: A pipeline is trustworthy only if the team agrees what each stage means.

items.label: New / contacted
items.detail: Record the enquiry and whether contact actually occurred.

items.label: Qualified
items.detail: Apply the written fit criteria consistently.

items.label: Demo / proposal
items.detail: Record the agreed next commitment and date.

items.label: Won / lost
items.detail: Confirm the outcome and capture an honest lost reason.

sections.takeaway: Do not move a lead forward just to make the dashboard look healthy.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. The pipeline: stages that mirror reality

sections.title: A score is a routing aid, not a truth
sections.explanation: These hypothetical scores show how the reading’s example thresholds route attention. They are not predicted conversion probabilities.

items.label: Lead A
items.detail: At least 60: personal follow-up under the example rule.

items.label: Lead B
items.detail: 30–59: nurture plus an agreed follow-up rhythm.

items.label: Lead C
items.detail: Below 30: lower-intensity permitted nurture.

sections.takeaway: Validate scoring against outcomes and fairness. Permission and suppression override a high score; a score is never consent.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.
sections.section: 3. Lead scoring: attention where it pays

sections.title: The follow-up loop ends with a recorded next step
sections.explanation: A contact attempt is not finished until the outcome and next action are visible to the team.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Check due actions and permission status.

items.label: Contact
items.detail: Use the appropriate channel and helpful context.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Log outcome, stage and relevant facts without unnecessary sensitive notes.

items.label: Schedule / close
items.detail: Assign the next action or close with a reason.

sections.takeaway: Stop repeated pursuit when the person opts out or the agreed contact policy is exhausted.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. The follow-up discipline

sections.title: Use the smallest tool that stays reliable
sections.explanation: Move up in tooling when shared ownership and control become hard, not because a larger product looks more professional.

items.label: Controlled sheet
items.detail: Useful for a small authorised team with clear fields and access.

items.label: Entry CRM
items.detail: Useful when reminders, ownership and a shared pipeline need stronger support.

items.label: Integrated system
items.detail: Useful when volume, controls and lifecycle hand-offs justify the complexity.

sections.takeaway: Plan access, retention, export and deletion before importing a real customer list.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A lead has a high score but has opted out of marketing. What wins?
checkpoint.answer: The opt-out and applicable contact restrictions win. A score only prioritises permitted actions; it cannot create permission.

sections.section: 5. Tooling at the right size

m7-t4.introduction: Use a purpose-first privacy workflow: collect less, explain clearly, record permission and make withdrawal work. Legal requirements must be checked for the actual context.

sections.title: Privacy begins before the form is built
sections.explanation: Treat privacy as an operating design, not a paragraph added after the campaign is ready.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: Write why the business needs each piece of information.

items.label: Minimise
items.detail: Remove fields that are not necessary for that purpose.

items.label: Inform / obtain permission
items.detail: Use the required notice and lawful permission for the actual context.

items.label: Manage
items.detail: Control access, retention, requests and withdrawal.

sections.takeaway: This diagram is a learning aid, not legal advice. Confirm current law, commencement stages and provider rules with the facilitator or qualified adviser.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The legal backbone, in plain terms

sections.title: Permission has a purpose and a channel
sections.explanation: The reason a person shared data determines what the business should do next.

items.label: Service communication
items.detail: Use information for the requested transaction or support.

items.label: Marketing permission
items.detail: Make the promotional purpose and channel clear and optional where required.

items.label: Partner use
items.detail: Do not silently extend the original purpose to unrelated organisations.

sections.takeaway: Agreeing to an order update is not automatically agreeing to promotional WhatsApp messages.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Consent types and what each permits

sections.title: A small compliant-flow design
sections.explanation: Make the entry, proof and exit visible as one connected process.

items.label: Explain
items.detail: Name the sender, purpose and expected type of communication.

items.label: Choose
items.detail: Use a clear, affirmative choice where consent is required.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Keep evidence of the wording, time, source and scope.

items.label: Withdraw
items.detail: Make the exit easy and propagate suppression to all relevant tools.

sections.takeaway: Test the unsubscribe route end-to-end. A visible link that does not change sending behaviour is not a working exit.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The compliant flows, built small

sections.title: A useful notice answers practical questions
sections.explanation: Plain language helps people understand the relationship. Completeness still depends on the applicable requirements.

items.label: What / why
items.detail: Explain the data collected and the purpose of use.

items.label: Who / access
items.detail: Explain relevant recipients and who operates the service.

items.label: How long
items.detail: State retention principles and the request route.

items.label: Choice / contact
items.detail: Explain withdrawal and the named help or grievance contact.

sections.takeaway: Do not promise a legal response deadline that the business has not checked and cannot meet.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. The privacy notice a small business can actually post

sections.title: Seven failures share a small set of causes
sections.explanation: Grouping the failure modes helps the team check the whole journey instead of only the signup box.

items.label: Invalid choice
items.detail: Bundled consent and pre-ticked boxes weaken the decision.

items.label: Broken exit
items.detail: A difficult unsubscribe and invisible request contact block control.

items.label: Unjustified reuse
items.detail: Purpose creep and bought or scraped lists break expectations.

items.label: Missing evidence
items.detail: Without records the business cannot show the permission it relied on.

sections.takeaway: Check collection, use, proof and exit together before approving a campaign.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A customer gave a number for delivery. Can it be added to a promotional broadcast by default?
checkpoint.answer: Do not assume so. Separate the delivery purpose from marketing, check the applicable legal and platform requirements, obtain the appropriate permission and provide a working exit.
